questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The informal economy and the tax base
questions.learningObjective: Explain how unrecorded trading narrows the declared tax base
questions.stem: Ticket OPS-441: A district legalises street vending but keeps no record of vendor income, so the team must explain what that does to the declared tax base of the city.

options.text: Vendors trade openly yet declare no income, so the tax base stays below actual economic activity
Legalising vending enlarges the declared base because every stall now sits on a licence list
options.misconception: counts a licence list as a record of taxable income

options.text: Nothing shifts because traders without invoices never draw on public services
options.misconception: believes service use is what makes activity taxable

options.text: The base shrinks only for as long as the pitch fee stays below market rent
options.misconception: assumes the fee level alone sets the size of the tax base

questions.explanation: Legal trading still leaves income unrecorded, so the declared base understates real activity. A licence list records permission, not income, and service use has no direct link to taxable capacity.
questions.hint: Ask what the tax register can actually observe.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a low local revenue share implies for local discretion
questions.stem: Ticket FIN-118: The dashboard shows the municipality funding 22 per cent of its own revenue locally, and the product owner asks what that share means for local discretion.

options.text: A small local share shows the council has no genuine need for its own revenue
options.misconception: treats transfer reliance as proof local tax is unnecessary

options.text: Most spending depends on decisions taken by higher tiers of government
The council directs 78 per cent of the budget because it allocates the grants it receives
options.misconception: reads a transfer share as if it were a discretionary share

options.text: Local taxpayers meet 22 per cent of the cost of every public service
options.misconception: confuses a revenue share with a service cost share

questions.explanation: A 22 per cent local share leaves 78 per cent of resources set by others, so local electoral choices change little. A revenue share says nothing about who pays for a given service.
questions.hint: Separate where money comes from from who decides it.

questions.learningObjective: Work out how an incomplete valuation register distorts modelled yield
questions.stem: Bug report BR-203: The pilot valuation register omits 30 per cent of dwellings, and the team must work out the effect on the modelled property-tax yield.

options.text: Yield falls proportionally, because every unregistered dwelling reduces the rate charged
options.misconception: confuses a capture rate with the rate charged per property

options.text: Yield rises, because unregistered dwellings are usually the most valuable in the district
options.misconception: assumes unrecorded dwellings are the most valuable

options.text: Yield per property is overstated, because fixed collection costs are spread over fewer recorded properties
Yield is unaffected, since a lower capture rate only shifts revenue between years
options.misconception: assumes collection costs stay fixed however many are reached

questions.explanation: With fewer properties on the register, the same staff and travel budget spreads across fewer billable properties, so net yield per property falls. The rate charged is separate from the owner count.
questions.hint: Think about the fixed cost of reaching each property.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe how duties assigned without funds appear in service delivery
questions.stem: Support thread ST-64: The district now runs libraries and waste collection but may not raise most of the money it spends, so the team must document the resulting fiscal problem.

answer.exemplar: The district has been assigned service obligations without the revenue or borrowing capacity that normally accompanies them. Spending is therefore set by rules it cannot influence, gaps appear when transfers fail to keep pace with costs, and unmet need is absorbed by service quality or by deferring maintenance.

questions.explanation: Unfunded mandates create a gap between duties and means. If transfers lag service costs, the shortfall shows up as deferred maintenance or thinner provision rather than an obvious budget line.
questions.hint: Look for where the shortfall becomes visible.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what settlement dispersion does to the cost of services

stimulus.body: The review compares two neighbourhoods of equal population, one compact and one spread across rural fringes. Per household, the compact area spends 18 per cent less on water, road maintenance and waste collection, and the differences are attributed to distance rather than to volume of service.

questions.stem: Ticket FIN-206: The delivery review compares two equal-population districts and the team must explain what the spending difference implies for planning at low density.

options.text: The compact district delivers a lower standard of service and therefore spends less
options.misconception: reads lower spending as poorer service, not higher unit cost

options.text: Waste collection dominates the difference while water and roads contribute nothing
options.misconception: single out one service as the cause when three are named

options.text: Population size, not settlement pattern, drives the whole spending gap
options.misconception: assumes equal population guarantees equal costs in services

options.text: Unit costs rise as settlement spreads out, so dispersed growth demands extra budget per resident

questions.explanation: Equal population with different spending points to distance, since travel and coverage per household rise when homes are scattered. Reading the gap as poorer service ignores the review.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which costs recur after a capital project is completed
questions.stem: Issue CR-58: The team must brief the council on why a new sports hall needs money after the ribbon is cut, beyond the cost of construction.

options.text: The hall keeps generating operating costs for staff, energy and upkeep for many years
Only construction matters, so the operating estimate can be set aside entirely
options.misconception: believes capital projects cost nothing once open

options.text: Operating costs are met by charging users, so the council faces no ongoing liability
options.misconception: assumes user charges cover a facility's full running cost

options.text: The running cost is a one-off settling charge once the opening month closes
options.misconception: treats a recurring cost as a single closing payment

questions.explanation: A sports hall commits the council to years of staffing, energy and maintenance, which the capital budget does not cover. User charges help but do not remove that liability.
questions.hint: Separate what building costs from what running it costs.

options.text: Debt levels must be rising because capital spending is so high
options.misconception: links a capital share to borrowing without debt data

options.text: Most of the budget is committed to building assets rather than running services
Services are receiving most of the budget because capital items are small
options.misconception: confuses the budget share with the size of a single item

options.text: The district spends more per year than it collects in revenue
options.misconception: assumes a high capital share must mean a revenue shortfall

questions.explanation: A 61 per cent capital share means most outlay builds assets rather than paying for current services. The share says nothing about whether collections cover spending.

questions.topic: Why a flat charge falls harder on the poor
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a flat charge weighs more heavily at low incomes
questions.stem: Support thread ST-77: Residents challenge a flat charge for a new waste fee, and the team must explain why the same payment weighs differently across incomes.

options.text: A flat fee falls hardest on the poor because poor households live in larger homes
options.misconception: assumes low incomes come with larger housing consumption

options.text: A flat fee is progressive because households with more income can afford to pay more
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the burden across incomes

options.text: A flat fee takes a larger share of a low income than of a high one, so it is regressive
A flat fee takes the same money from everyone, so it is by definition equitable
options.misconception: treats equal payment amounts as equal burdens across incomes

questions.explanation: A flat fee consumes a bigger proportion of a small income than of a large one, which makes it regressive. Equal amounts charged are not equal burdens, and household size does not reverse that pattern.
questions.hint: Compare the fee with each household's income.

questions.stem: Chat request CH-145: A residents' assembly votes on a small park budget, and the team must explain what makes the vote binding rather than advisory.

options.text: The assembly has legal authority to levy a tax on the district
options.misconception: assumes a participatory body carries taxing powers

options.text: The council always adopts assembly decisions regardless of its own rules
options.misconception: assumes any council decision must follow any public vote

options.text: The vote counted because it took place in a public meeting
options.misconception: treats publicity as the source of the council's obligation

options.text: The council committed in advance to carry out the voted items in the budget

questions.explanation: Binding force comes from the council's pre-commitment to implement the voted items, not from the meeting itself. Recording them in the budget makes the outcome more than advice.
questions.hint: Look for what the council committed to in advance.

questions.learningObjective: State why widening a tax base requires collection capacity as well as coverage
questions.stem: Work log WL-33: The team must explain to a council committee why a thriving street market produces taxable activity that never appears in the accounts.

options.text: Cash turnover from unregistered stalls stays outside the tax net even when the market is busy
Market activity is taxable only if stalls operate on council-owned land
options.misconception: ties tax liability to land ownership rather than to income

options.text: A busy market generates more tax simply because more people pass through it
options.misconception: assumes footfall increases collections for the council

options.text: Unregistered income becomes taxable once traders buy local goods
options.misconception: thinks spending the cash pulls the seller into the tax net

questions.explanation: Informal sellers earn income that never passes through a register, so the tax net captures only the formal slice of a busy market. Land location and footfall do not create taxable income.

questions.learningObjective: Assess how exposed a budget is when transfers dominate revenue
questions.stem: Ticket FIN-340: Revenue data shows local sources covering 41 per cent of district outlay and transfers 59 per cent, and the team must judge how exposed the budget is.

options.text: Local exposure is zero, since locally raised revenue never changes
options.misconception: treats locally raised revenue as immune to any change

options.text: A swing in transferred funding would hit most of the budget, with little local money to absorb it
Only the 41 per cent is at risk, because transfers are legally guaranteed each year
options.misconception: assumes transferred money is fixed in every year

options.text: A 59 per cent transfer share means the district can raise most of what it spends
options.misconception: reads the transfer share as a locally controlled share

questions.explanation: With 59 per cent of the budget set elsewhere, a change in transferred funding reaches most spending lines. The locally controlled 41 per cent offers little room to absorb a shock, so exposure is high.

questions.learningObjective: Judge the limits of a yield projection built on a partial register
questions.stem: Bug report BR-511: A register of 42,000 properties is found to miss 12,000 dwellings, and the team must work out what that means for the yield model.

options.text: Yield is too low, because the register adds households that pay nothing
options.misconception: mistakes extra recorded entries for extra paying households

options.text: The register can be left as it is, since the count is already precise
options.misconception: confuses a count of records with a count of accurate records

options.text: The apparent yield per property is too high, since costs are spread over too few captured households
The shortfall is harmless, because unregistered dwellings are charged directly
options.misconception: assumes uncounted properties are billed outside the register

questions.explanation: Thirty thousand captured properties carry the collection cost against 42,000 real dwellings, so the modelled yield per property is inflated. The gap is a revenue gap, not a footnote.
questions.hint: Compare the number of records with the number of homes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how devolved duties without funds should be presented to decision makers
questions.stem: Support thread ST-140: A new duty is transferred to the district without matching funds, and the team must draft the explanation that goes to the finance committee.

answer.exemplar: The duty has been devolved without the revenue that previously paid for it, so the district must either raise local charges that residents did not expect, draw on reserves that fund other services, or quietly cut the standard of delivery. Because spending is mandatory but revenue is discretionary, the shortfall appears as a service reduction rather than as a budget failure.

questions.explanation: A duty without funds forces a choice between new local charges, reserves and reduced service. Spending is compulsory while raising revenue is not, so pressure lands on delivery and on other services.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the equation the district can change.

questions.stem: Ticket OPS-633: The water cost study compares three settlements and the team must explain what the figures imply about approving scattered housing.

options.text: The three costs reflect differences in tariff design rather than in network layout
options.misconception: blames tariff choices for a difference in network cost

options.text: Only the rural figure matters, because the edge settlement is really part of the compact one
options.misconception: dismisses one settlement's cost rather than the pattern

options.text: Network cost per resident falls as a settlement spreads, because the pipes are shared
options.misconception: assumes longer shared mains cut the cost of a connection

options.text: Approval policy can push development into patterns that permanently raise the cost of serving each resident

questions.explanation: Costs rise with dispersion because each remote household needs its own share of mains. Since networks last for decades, approval rules today set a permanent cost per resident.

options.misconception: assumes structures without services carry no upkeep

options.text: Only vehicles add maintenance, so a footbridge escapes the running budget
options.misconception: thinks upkeep depends on what traffic a structure carries

options.misconception: reads a large capital share as under-capital spending

options.text: A flat charge hurts the poor least, since they use less water once connected
options.misconception: assumes usage savings from a connection outweigh a charge

options.text: Flat charges always shift money towards poorer households over time

options.misconception: confuses equal prices with equal shares of income

questions.learningObjective: Explain why service erosion precedes any visible budget gap
questions.stem: Support thread ST-166: The team must describe for the county office why residents notice service cuts long before the budget shows any gap.

answer.exemplar: Resident-facing services are the visible edge of a budget whose pressures first appear in maintenance deferrals and staffing vacancies. questions.explanation: Obligations exceed available funds, so the adjustment happens at the softest point first: deferrals and vacancies. Residents see thinner services, which hides the fiscal cause from them.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why a flat charge falls harder on the poor
questions.learningObjective: Compare the burden of weight-based and flat waste charges
questions.stem: Support thread ST-181: A proposal replaces per-household waste charges with a per-kilogram weight charge, and the team must advise the council on who bears the cost.

options.text: A weight charge has the same distributional effect as a flat fee because prices rise
options.misconception: ignores that payments change with the waste thrown

options.text: Weight-based charging is progressive because wealthier households generate more rubbish
options.misconception: assumes income tracks waste weight without evidence

options.text: A weight charge makes heavy waste households pay more and light waste households pay less than a flat fee
A weight charge always lowers the bill for every household regardless of output
options.misconception: assumes all households cut waste by the same amount

questions.explanation: Weight-based charging links payment to the amount thrown, so households differ in the shape of their burden against a flat fee. Whether poorer households gain depends on waste output against income.
questions.hint: Compare the payment rule, not just the price.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the binding power of a vote affects participation

stimulus.body: Participation fell in the third round after the council removed the funding guarantee for assemblies below a set size of proposals. Assemblies with fewer than 40 proposals received a recommendation rather than a binding allocation.

questions.stem: Chat request CH-260: The team must explain what the participation data suggests about how binding the process is.

options.text: Participation fell because residents were satisfied with the previous results
options.misconception: reads a fall in participation as satisfaction with outcomes

options.text: The funding guarantee was a decorative feature with no effect on attendance
options.misconception: assumes a formal guarantee plays no part in drawing people

options.text: Small assemblies attract fewer residents because they meet in smaller rooms
options.misconception: explains the fall by room size rather than by binding power

options.text: Participation tracks binding power, so removing it for small groups removes their voice

questions.explanation: Participation fell precisely where the funding guarantee was withdrawn, so people respond to whether the vote changes outcomes. Satisfaction with earlier results would not explain that fall.
questions.hint: Notice what changed at the same time as the fall.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The informal economy and the tax base
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish tax coverage from tax collection capacity
questions.stem: Ticket OPS-755: The team must explain why widening the declared tax base requires more than adding businesses to the register.

options.text: Coverage only helps if the authority can inspect, value and collect from what it registers
Adding names to the register automatically produces collectable revenue
options.misconception: assumes registration turns recorded firms into paying firms

options.text: Tax bases depend solely on the number of firms, never on enforcement
options.misconception: treats the count of registered firms as the whole collection

options.text: Inspection capacity is a matter for the treasury and concerns nobody else
options.misconception: treats enforcement capacity as irrelevant to the base

questions.explanation: A wider register raises the ceiling on collections, but only if the authority can find, value and bill what it records. Without enforcement capacity, coverage adds work without revenue.
questions.hint: Ask what stands between a record and a payment.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why identical spending can coexist with very different local revenue
questions.stem: Ticket FIN-701: The dashboard compares two districts with identical spending of 50,000,000, and the team must explain why one raises 12,000,000 locally and the other 30,000,000.

options.text: Local revenue differences are explained entirely by population size
options.misconception: explains a revenue gap by population while spending is equal

options.text: Local revenue differs because the tax base, rates and collection effort differ, not because spending differs
The district raising less locally must be spending badly on administration
options.misconception: assumes low local collection signals administrative failure

options.text: Spending at 50,000,000 implies a fixed local revenue share for every district
options.misconception: treats equal spending as proof of equal local revenue

questions.explanation: Holding spending constant isolates the revenue side, where differences in base, rates and effort produce different local totals. Neither population nor spending can vary here.
questions.hint: Notice which variable has been held constant.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Property tax and the limits of a register
questions.learningObjective: Assess the effect of transactions missing from the valuation roll
questions.stem: Bug report BR-702: A register update found 8,100 property transactions that never reached the valuation roll, and the team must judge the consequence.

options.text: The shortfall inflates the roll, making the district appear to collect more
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the error in the valuation roll

options.text: The register can be repaired at year end with no effect on collections
options.misconception: assumes the roll can be fixed later without revenue loss

options.text: The roll understates the taxable base, so fewer correctly valued properties carry the collection
The transactions have no effect, since only current owners are taxable
options.misconception: confuses liability to pay with the valuation on the roll

questions.explanation: Missing transactions mean the roll carries stale or absent valuations, so the base is understated and collection rests on too few assessed properties. Waiting until year end recovers nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what the roll now gets wrong about value.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Advise on who should carry the cost of a newly transferred duty
questions.stem: Support thread ST-210: The county proposes a new duty for districts to certify building safety, and the team must draft the note on who should carry the cost.

answer.exemplar: Certification creates inspection, record-keeping and training costs that arrive with the duty rather than with the money. If the county transfers no new revenue for the work, districts must fund certification from existing sources, which means either higher charges on residents, slower investment elsewhere, or a certification backlog that leaves unsafe buildings uninspected.

questions.explanation: New duties bring running costs. Without matched funding, districts absorb certification from existing budgets, appearing as higher charges, displaced investment or a backlog of uninspected buildings.
questions.hint: Check whether the duty arrived with any money.

questions.topic: Capital spending as a share of a budget
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the capital share of a budget from its two parts
questions.stem: Task TSK-2046: A council must find how much of a 20,000,000 budget is capital when capital projects total 11,000,000, and the team must express it as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Capital is 11,000,000 out of a total of 20,000,000, and 11 divided by 20 is 0.55, so 55 per cent. The remaining 45 per cent is the revenue share that pays for running services.
questions.hint: Divide the capital total by the whole budget.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why edge development can raise costs for existing households
questions.stem: Ticket OPS-820: The team must explain why approving a single housing estate on the edge of a small town can raise costs for the whole district.

options.text: Edge estates are cheaper for everyone because land there is unbuilt and free
options.misconception: assumes undeveloped land carries no extension cost

options.text: Only new households pay more, since existing routes are never extended
options.misconception: ignores that existing households share the extended networks

options.text: Concentrated development reduces infrastructure cost because it shortens networks
options.misconception: reverses the link between concentration and network length

options.text: Edge housing pushes roads, water and waste routes further, so service cost per household rises

questions.explanation: Extending routes to an edge estate lengthens the shared networks every household relies on, so cost per household rises across the district. Existing residents bear part of that cost.
questions.hint: Think about who shares the extended routes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify which costs belong in the annual running budget
questions.stem: Issue CR-183: A new market hall adds to the authority's annual costs, and the team must identify what belongs in the running budget.

options.text: Cleaning, security, utilities and building maintenance, which recur every year the hall is open
Only the market hall's construction cost, which was funded by capital borrowing
options.misconception: puts a completed capital project inside the running budget

options.text: Refuse collection, because the hall's own costs are covered by stallholders
options.misconception: assumes concession income covers a building's operating cost

options.text: Advertising income, because the hall will certainly attract sponsorship
options.misconception: counts uncertain sponsorship as guaranteed revenue

questions.explanation: Cleaning, security, utilities and upkeep recur annually and belong in the revenue budget, whereas construction was a one-off capital item. Stallholder income may offset part of the bill.
questions.hint: Ask which costs arrive again next year.

questions.topic: Capital spending as a share of a budget
questions.learningObjective: Explain a change in the composition of spending between two years
questions.stem: Work log WL-112: The team compares a year when capital was 64 per cent of spending with one where it was 29 per cent, and must describe what the shift reflects.

options.text: The two years differ only in how the accounts were labelled
options.misconception: dismisses a large composition change as a labelling artefact

options.text: The district moved between building new assets and maintaining or operating what it already owns
The district's total spending fell by half between the two years
options.misconception: reads a changing share as a changing level of spending

options.text: Revenue collections fell when the capital share fell in the second year
options.misconception: assumes capital and revenue shares must move together

questions.explanation: A fall from 64 to 29 per cent capital means the weight of the budget moved from new assets toward running and upkeep. Shares can move sharply while the level of spending does not.
questions.hint: Distinguish composition from total level.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why a flat charge falls harder on the poor
questions.learningObjective: Assess the effect of a flat permit fee on the smallest traders
questions.stem: Ticket FIN-788: A flat permit fee of 90 is charged for market stalls, and the team must assess its effect on the smallest traders.

options.text: The fee cannot affect small traders since permits are optional for stalls
options.misconception: ignores that traders still sell even without a permit

options.text: Small traders are protected because market regulation sets a fee ceiling for them
options.misconception: assumes a regulatory ceiling exists for the authority's fee

options.text: Small traders with low turnover pay a large share of their income for the permit
Small traders pay a smaller share of income because the fee is the same for everyone
options.misconception: confuses a common fee with a common share of income

questions.explanation: A fixed fee takes a large proportion of a small turnover, so it is proportionally harder on the smallest traders. Traders who evade the permit still sell, concentrating the burden on those who comply.
questions.hint: Compare the fee with the smallest traders' earnings.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what makes residents return to a participatory budget

stimulus.body: Two districts used the same participatory rules. In the first, allocations were published and the council met its funding commitment in every round. In the second, allocations were published but never funded. Repeat participation fell by two thirds in the second district and stayed level in the first.

questions.stem: Chat request CH-305: The team must identify what the comparison shows about why people take part.

options.text: People return because voting itself is enjoyable regardless of funding
options.misconception: assumes voting is the only thing that sustains participation

options.text: The two districts differ so much that no comparison of participation is possible
options.misconception: declines comparison because the districts are not identical

options.text: Participation in the second district fell because notices were not published
options.misconception: contradicts the record that allocations were published

options.text: People return when the money they influence actually arrives, not merely when it is voted on

questions.explanation: Both districts published allocations and used the same rules, so the only difference was whether the money arrived, and participation collapsed where it did not. Notices cannot explain that.
questions.hint: Find the one thing that differed between them.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The informal economy and the tax base
questions.learningObjective: Predict the revenue effect of inspecting small informal traders
questions.stem: Ticket OPS-905: A new inspection regime targets the least visible part of the economy, and the team must explain the expected revenue effect.

options.text: Inspecting small traders should bring unrecorded income into the tax base, though it also costs staff time
Inspecting small traders raises revenue with no cost because the paperwork is trivial
options.misconception: ignores the ongoing cost of an inspection regime

options.text: Inspection discourages trading so much that recorded income falls afterwards
options.misconception: confuses a short compliance dip with a permanent loss

options.text: Small traders pay no tax at any scale, so inspection cannot change collections
options.misconception: treats informality as if it meant total tax immunity

questions.explanation: Enforcement widens the recorded base, but it is not free: each regime carries recurring staff and administrative cost. A short dip in activity while traders adapt is not a permanent loss.
questions.hint: Include both the gain and the running cost.

questions.learningObjective: Summarise what a rising local revenue share means for control over spending
questions.stem: Ticket FIN-830: The district's own revenue now stands at 28 per cent of the total, up from 12 per cent five years ago, and the team must summarise the change.

options.text: Residents now pay a much higher tax rate than they did five years ago
options.misconception: infers a tax rate change from a share of total revenue

options.text: A larger part of the budget is now under the district's own control
The district's total spending has risen by sixteen percentage points
options.misconception: confuses a share change with an absolute spending rise

options.text: Transferred funding has grown faster than local revenue over the period
options.misconception: ignores the direction of the change the data actually shows

questions.explanation: The local share rose from 12 to 28 per cent, so the district now controls a larger part of its own resources and can be more responsive to local voters. The share says nothing about tax rates.
questions.hint: Read the trend, not the absolute amounts.

questions.topic: Property tax and the limits of a register
questions.learningObjective: Explain why missing register entries are a revenue issue rather than a clerical one
questions.stem: Bug report BR-811: A township's valuation roll lists 61 per cent of dwellings, and the team must explain why the missing records are not simply a clerical detail.

options.text: Missing properties are low value, so their absence barely affects the yield
options.misconception: assumes unrecorded properties are the least valuable

options.text: The register only matters for postal purposes, not for charging
options.misconception: believes the register serves only postal purposes

options.text: A missing property is an uncharged property, so the gap is a direct loss of declared revenue
The missing records are clerical and can be ignored until the next audit
options.misconception: treats a revenue gap as a clerical matter with no effect

questions.explanation: An absent property is a property that is never billed, so each gap is revenue the authority has decided not to collect. Nothing in the register shows the missing entries are low-value ones.
questions.hint: Ask what one missing entry costs the authority.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a capital award can still create a funding gap afterwards
questions.stem: Support thread ST-233: The team must explain why the district asked for a grant yet still faced a funding gap on a project it was given.

answer.exemplar: A grant usually covers capital construction but not the staff, energy or maintenance that follow. The project therefore absorbs running costs into a revenue line that was already committed, so the authority can end up with a building it cannot afford to open or maintain. The gap appears after the ribbon is cut, which is why a successful capital award can still create fiscal stress.

questions.explanation: Capital grants often omit operating costs. The asset then draws on a revenue line already committed, so stress appears only once the facility is in use, not when the award is announced.
questions.hint: Ask what the award actually pays for.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the annual repayment of a long-term loan at a stated rate
questions.stem: Task TSK-2047: A district needs to know the yearly repayment on a 250,000 loan for a depot over 25 years at 4 per cent annual interest, and the team must calculate it.
questions.explanation: The annual principal share is 250,000 over twenty-five years, so 10,000, and interest on 250,000 at 4 per cent adds another 10,000. The yearly repayment is therefore 20,000 on a simple-interest basis.
questions.hint: Split the loan into principal share and interest.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the per-household cost relationship that the settlement audit supports

stimulus.body: The audit compared per-household spending on the same service set in four settlements. Two compact settlements spent 210 and 224 units per household. Two dispersed settlements of the same household count spent 305 and 338 units per household.

questions.stem: Ticket FIN-905: The audit figures are tabulated for the council and the team must state what they support.

options.text: Per-household cost falls with dispersion because scattered routes serve more stops
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the relationship with dispersion

options.text: The differences are explained by household numbers, which differ between the settlements
options.misconception: invokes household numbers that the audit holds constant

options.text: Spending per household is a fixed norm that every settlement must meet
options.misconception: assumes a norm exists that overrides physical layout

options.text: Per-household cost rises with dispersion at comparable household counts

questions.explanation: Both compact settlements spend less per household than both dispersed ones while household counts are held constant, so dispersion moves the cost. A norm cannot explain the difference between places.
questions.hint: Note what the audit holds constant.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a new depot reshapes long-run expenditure
questions.stem: Issue CR-210: A new depot raises weekly utilities, and the team must explain how that changes the shape of the district's long-run costs.

options.text: The district trades a one-off capital outlay for a permanent addition to yearly running expenditure
The depot costs the same each year as it cost to build, so nothing changes
options.misconception: assumes the yearly running cost equals the capital cost

options.text: Utilities for a depot are paid by users, so the district's budget is unaffected
options.misconception: assumes building users absorb a building's utility cost

options.text: The one-off capital outlay continues every year, which is the larger burden
options.misconception: reverses which element of the cost recurs over time

questions.explanation: The depot converts a single large capital payment into a permanent addition to annual revenue expenditure, which is the structural change the budget must absorb. Users may offset some utilities.
questions.hint: Compare the shape of the two cost streams.

options.misconception: treats equal service received as evidence of equal burden

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out why a mismatch between duties and revenue is structural
questions.stem: Support thread ST-260: The team must set out for new colleagues what makes a responsibility unmatched by revenue a structural problem.

answer.exemplar: Structural problems persist because no single decision creates them. The duty is assigned in one place and the money that supported it in another, so neither the councillor who promised the service nor the official who holds the budget can resolve the gap alone. Each year the shortfall is absorbed in maintenance, staffing or charges, which delays the point at which the mismatch has to be faced.

questions.explanation: The duty and its funding are decided separately, so no single actor owns the mismatch. Each year the gap is absorbed through deferrals and staffing, pushing the decision further away.
questions.hint: Ask who can actually close a gap like this.

questions.hint: Take the grant share away from the project cost.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the long-run budget effect of changing how a public space is used
questions.stem: Issue CR-244: A new public square replaces a car park, and the team must assess the long-run budget effect of the change.

options.text: The square is cost-neutral, since it replaces an area that also needed upkeep
options.misconception: assumes a revenue asset and a cost asset cost the same

options.text: Replacing parking with a square increases revenue because more visitors stay longer
options.misconception: assumes longer visits always produce net additional income

options.text: One-off construction costs dominate, so running costs can be ignored for ten years
options.misconception: treats capital outlay as if it were the only relevant cost

options.text: Space given to the square removes parking income and adds maintenance costs that recur each year

questions.explanation: Converting revenue-generating parking into a public square swaps an income stream for recurring upkeep and staffing costs, which matters over years. Longer visits do not produce net income.
questions.hint: Compare the recurring effects on both sides.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Capital spending as a share of a budget
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an undrawn contingency line within a budget
questions.stem: Work log WL-170: The audit shows that 12 per cent of the budget sits in a contingency line that was never drawn, and the team must explain what that implies.

options.text: Unspent contingency signals a cushion for shocks rather than resources available for spending now
Twelve per cent of the budget is unrecorded money that could be spent immediately
options.misconception: treats an undrawn contingency as spendable revenue

options.text: The contingency proves that forecast service costs were always too low
options.misconception: reads a reserve as proof that forecasts were pessimistic

options.text: Contingency funds are held for capital projects and never for revenue shortfalls
options.misconception: assumes contingency is reserved only for capital schemes

questions.explanation: An undrawn contingency is a reserve held against unforeseen shocks, not money available for planned spending. Whether it can absorb a shortfall depends on its rules.
questions.hint: Ask what the reserve is held for.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why a flat charge falls harder on the poor
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an identical flat charge lands on two different income groups

stimulus.body: For two household groups with the same weekly shop, the lower-income group spends 38 per cent of its income on the shop, while the higher-income group spends 9 per cent. Both were quoted the same flat charge of 45 for a community water scheme.

questions.stem: Chat request CH-400: The survey is discussed in a residents' meeting and the team must explain how the same charge lands on the two groups.

options.text: Because the groups buy the same goods, the flat charge must also affect them equally
options.misconception: assumes identical consumption implies identical burdens

options.text: The flat charge takes a far larger share of the lower-income group's income than of the other group's
Both groups pay the same 45, so both feel the charge in exactly the same way
options.misconception: confuses equal amounts with equal proportional burden

options.text: The charge matters more to the lower-income group only because it shops more often
options.misconception: attaches the difference to shopping habits, not income

questions.explanation: Identical shop burdens of 38 and 9 per cent show the two groups have very different incomes, so the same 45 is a very different proportion of each. Equal prices do not produce equal burdens.
questions.hint: Use the survey percentages to infer the incomes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why identical rules can produce unequal participation outcomes

stimulus.body: The review found that proposals from lower-income areas were technically weaker because residents lacked drafting support, and that the scoring panel gave such proposals lower marks. Funding rules were applied identically to all areas.

questions.stem: Chat request CH-450: The review findings are published and the team must explain what they suggest about the fairness of the process.

options.text: The findings show that participation should be limited to areas that draft well
options.misconception: draws a restriction on participation from a drafting gap

options.text: Because the rules were identical, the differences in results prove bias in the panel
options.misconception: concludes deliberate bias from a finding about drafting

options.text: Identical rules can still produce unequal outcomes when some groups cannot afford drafting help
Equal rules guarantee equal outcomes, so the scoring differences must come from the residents
options.misconception: assumes identical treatment guarantees identical results

questions.explanation: Applying the same rules to groups with different capacities to use them produces different results, which the review documents. That is a design fault, not proof that the panel was biased.
questions.hint: Separate unequal capacity from unequal treatment.
